ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in Figure 10, a block Q is sleeved on a horizontal smooth long rod; one end of a light rope passing over a small light smooth ring suspended at point O is connected to Q, and the other end suspends a block P. Let the angle between the left part of the light rope and the horizontal direction be θ, and initially θ is very small. Now P and Q are released simultaneously from rest. Regarding the subsequent motion of P and Q, which of the following statements is correct (　　)
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: When θ＝90°, the speed of Q is maximum

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in Figure 10, a block Q is sleeved on a horizontal smooth long rod; one end of a light rope passing over a small light smooth ring suspended at point O is connected to Q, and the other end suspends a block P. Let the angle between the left part of the light rope and the horizontal direction be θ, and initially θ is very small. Now P and Q are released simultaneously from rest. During the subsequent motion, when θ is what value is the speed of Q maximum?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: When θ=90°, the speed of Q is maximum
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a horizontal long rod, and block Q is sleeved on the rod and is located to the left of the point vertically below point O; above there is a fixed suspended small smooth ring O. One end of the light rope is connected to Q, going obliquely upward around ring O; the angle between the left oblique segment of the light rope and the horizontal rod is marked as θ; the other segment of the light rope goes vertically downward from O, with block P suspended at its end. Reasoning: Let the vertical distance from ring O to the horizontal rod be h, and the horizontal distance from Q to the point directly below O be x; then the left oblique rope length l=√(x²+h²). Since θ in the figure is the angle between the oblique rope and the horizontal direction, sinθ=h/l, so l=h/sinθ. The total length of the light rope is unchanged, and the increase in the vertical rope length at the P end is equal to the decrease in the length of the left oblique rope; therefore the falling distance of P is equal to the decrease in oblique rope length. Differentiate the constraint relation: l=√(x²+h²), so |dl/dt|=(x/l)|dx/dt|=v_Q cosθ; hence the speed of P is v_P=v_Q cosθ. The system is smooth, the light rope is light, and the ring is smooth, so mechanical energy is conserved. If the initial oblique rope length is l_0, then the decrease in gravitational potential energy of P, m_P g(l_0-l), is transformed into the kinetic energy of P and Q: m_P g(l_0-l)=1/2 m_Q v_Q²+1/2 m_P v_P²=1/2(m_Q+m_P cos²θ)v_Q². Substituting l=h/sinθ gives v_Q²=2m_P g(l_0-h/sinθ)/(m_Q+m_P cos²θ). In the process from the initially very small θ increasing to 90°, h/sinθ continuously decreases, so l_0-h/sinθ continuously increases; meanwhile cos²θ continuously decreases, so the denominator m_Q+m_P cos²θ continuously decreases. Therefore v_Q², that is, the speed of Q, continuously increases, and is maximum when θ reaches 90°.
